summary_html: Family agrees to a **voluntary service plan**—counseling, substance-use treatment, parenting classes—designed to correct conditions without court compulsion. Federal law prioritizes family preservation through prevention and support services.

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: The court reversed a termination of parental rights because the trial court never prescribed written norms of parental conduct the father was expected to meet, and it announced prospectively that a termination-seeking party must prove parental potential for harm by clear and convincing evidence.
key_cases.relevance: Sets the constitutional floor for any correction-of-conditions plan: services a parent is asked to accept voluntarily must be translated into conduct norms clear enough to be complied with.
key_cases.quote: Judicial clarity in the prescribed norms of parental conduct is essential to the preservation of the procedural safeguards mandated by state and federal due process.

key_cases.holding: The court affirmed termination, holding DHS made reasonable reunification efforts despite the absence of visitation the children refused, that clear and convincing evidence supported the jury's verdict, and that trial counsel was effective.
key_cases.relevance: The opinion catalogues the counseling and other voluntary services DHS supplied and treats their provision as the measure of adequate front-end effort.
key_cases.quote: We find the district court did not abuse its discretion when it found that DHS made reasonable efforts toward reunification.

key_cases.court: Court of Civil Appeals of Oklahoma
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed the denial of a new trial, holding ICWA's active-efforts requirement did not apply because no existing Indian family relationship would be broken up, and alternatively that clear and convincing evidence showed active efforts were made and had failed.
key_cases.relevance: Simmers marks the outer limit of the duty to offer remedial and rehabilitative services to a tribal-member parent who never had a relationship with the child.
key_cases.quote: we conclude § 1912(d) of ICWA is inapplicable because there was no relationship or Indian family entity to breakup

key_cases.case_name: In the Matter of Baby Boy L.
key_cases.holding: The court reversed an order declaring an Indian child eligible for adoption without the father's consent, abandoning the judicially created existing Indian family exception in light of amendments to the Oklahoma ICWA and expressly overruling In re S.C., Baby Boy D and D.M.J.
key_cases.relevance: Baby Boy L. removes the escape hatch a state agency could otherwise use to avoid ICWA's remedial and rehabilitative service obligations toward a tribal-member parent.
key_cases.quote: the "existing Indian family exception" is no longer a viable doctrine applicable in Oklahoma insofar as Indian child custody proceedings are concerned

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court reversed, holding that ICWA section 1912(f) does not apply where the Indian parent never had custody, that section 1912(d)'s remedial-efforts requirement applies only where termination would precipitate the breakup of an Indian family, and that section 1915(a) does not bar an adoption when no preferred placement has come forward.
key_cases.relevance: Adoptive Couple is the controlling federal limit on when ICWA requires remedial and rehabilitative services to be offered to a tribal-member parent before rights are severed.
key_cases.quote: Consistent with the statutory text, we hold that §1912(d) applies only in cases where an Indian family's "breakup" would be precipitated by the termination of the parent's rights.
